title: Tailoring CKLA Knowledge for Second Grade
author: Daniel Kliger
summary: Second grade teacher Daniel Kliger describes how he modifies the Knowledge strand of Core Knowledge Language Arts, which he credits for building background knowledge but finds weak on instruction and content design. His main complaint is that lower elementary CKLA has too little reading, because most Knowledge lessons are read-alouds and the Skills block offers only about fifteen minutes of decodable text. His fix is to have students read the knowledge texts, so he copies read-aloud text into a document, revises it himself or with an LLM, strips weak historical fiction, and adds line numbers and section questions. In class he uses whole-class FASE reading and, later in the year, reading partners. He closes by arguing that CKLA reverses priorities, since fluency enables knowledge acquisition more than the reverse.
points: Kliger finds CKLA Knowledge strong on content but short on actual student reading in grades K-2, where lessons are mostly teacher read-alouds.
He converts read-alouds into student texts, revising them with an LLM to clarify cause and effect and remove weak historical fiction.
A numbered-line template and section questions make it easier to direct students to specific places in the text.
He uses FASE reading as a whole class early on and shifts to reading partners as the year goes on, so everyone reads more.
He argues fluency makes knowledge easier to acquire more than knowledge improves fluency, so CKLA's balance is counterproductive.
quotes: In the lower elementary grades, CKLA doesn’t have enough reading. For second grade, most Knowledge lessons involve a read-aloud but no actual reading.

CKLA seems to believe that it’s harmful for kids to read any text that exceeds the complexity of the phonics they’ve been explicitly taught. This view of literacy development is both limited and limiting.
Fortunately, the solution, to my mind, is fairly obvious: have the kids read the knowledge texts instead of just listening to them.
The writing presented to children in CKLA materials is often so bad it has threatened to change my opinion on AI-generated content.
I have a template to keep lines numbered, which makes it easier to direct students to a specific part of each page.
Reading fluency accelerates knowledge acquisition far more than acquiring knowledge facilitates reading fluency.
When knowledge-building comes at the cost of being a strong reader, it cannibalizes much of its promised benefit.
